chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: One thing about his management sometimes troubled Nicholas: his quick temper, combined with his old hussar habit of settling things with his fists. At first he saw nothing wrong with this, but in the second year of his marriage an incident occurred that changed his view.

One summer he had sent for the village elder from Bogucharovo, a man who had taken over when Dron died and who was accused of dishonesty and various irregularities. Nicholas went out onto the porch to question him, and immediately after the elder's first answers, the sound of shouting and blows could be heard from the porch. Returning to the house for lunch, Nicholas went up to his wife, who sat with her embroidery frame, and began telling her—as he usually did—everything that had occupied him that morning. Among other things, he mentioned the Bogucharovo village elder. Countess Mary, turning red, then pale, and pressing her lips together, sat in the same position, offering no reply to her husband.
"The insolent scoundrel!" he cried, getting heated all over again just remembering. "If he'd told me he was drunk and couldn't see straight... But what's the matter, Mary?" he suddenly asked.
Countess Mary raised her head and tried to speak, but quickly looked down again, her lips trembling.
"Why, what is it, my dearest?"
Plain Countess Mary always looked better when she cried. She never cried from pain or frustration—only from sorrow or compassion—and when she wept, her radiant eyes took on an irresistible beauty.
The moment Nicholas took her hand, she could no longer hold back and began to cry.
"Nicholas, I saw it... he was wrong, but why did you... Nicholas!" She covered her face with her hands.

Nicholas said nothing. He turned crimson, left her side, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but couldn't immediately agree in his heart that what he had done since childhood—what he considered perfectly normal—was wrong.
"Mary," he said softly, going up to her, "it will never happen again. I give you my word. Never," he repeated in a trembling voice, like a boy asking for forgiveness.
The tears flowed even faster from the countess's eyes. She took his hand and kissed it.
"Nicholas, when did you break your cameo?" she asked, wanting to change the subject, and looking at his finger where he wore a ring with a cameo of Laocoon's head.

"Today—the same business. Oh, Mary, don't remind me of it!" And again he flushed. "I give you my word of honor it won't happen again. And let this always be a reminder," he said, pointing to the broken ring.

After that, whenever in discussions with his village elders or stewards the blood rushed to his face and his fists began to clench, Nicholas would turn the broken ring on his finger and drop his eyes before whoever was making him angry. But he still lost his temper once or twice a year and would then go to his wife and confess, promising once again that this was really the last time.
"Mary, you must despise me!" he would say. "I deserve it."
"You should just leave—walk away at once—if you don't feel strong enough to control yourself," she would reply sadly, trying to comfort her husband.

Among the local gentry, Nicholas was respected but not liked. He didn't concern himself with the interests of his own class, and so some thought him proud and others thought him stupid. The entire summer, from spring sowing to harvest, he was busy with farming. In autumn he devoted himself to hunting with the same businesslike seriousness, going off with his dogs for a month or two at a time. In winter he visited his other villages and spent his time reading. The books he read were mainly historical. Every year he bought a set number of serious books and made it a rule to read them all. He would sit in his study with a grave expression, devoting himself to this reading—a task he had initially imposed on himself as a duty but which later became a habit providing him with a special kind of satisfaction and the awareness that he was engaged in something important. Except for occasional business trips, he spent the winter at home, entering fully into the family life and the details of his relationship with his wife and children. He was growing closer to his wife, discovering new spiritual treasures in her every day.

From the time of his marriage, Sonya had lived in his house. Before that, Nicholas had told his wife everything that had passed between himself and Sonya, blaming himself and praising her. He had asked Princess Mary to be gentle and kind to his cousin. She felt her husband's generosity; she also felt her own guilt toward Sonya; she recognized that her own wealth had influenced Nicholas's choice; she could find nothing to blame Sonya for, and wanted to love her. But she could not. She could not, and sometimes her soul harbored unkind feelings toward Sonya that she could not overcome.
Once she had a conversation with her friend Natasha about Sonya and about her own injustice toward her.
"You know," said Natasha, "you've read the Gospels a lot—there's a passage that fits Sonya exactly."
"What?" asked Countess Mary, surprised.

"'To him who has, more shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away.' Remember? She's the one who has not. Why? I don't know. Maybe she lacks selfishness—I don't know—but from her, things are taken away, and everything has been taken away. Sometimes I feel terribly sorry for her. I used to desperately want Nicholas to marry her, but I always had a feeling it would never happen. She's a sterile flower—you know, like in strawberry plants? Sometimes I feel sorry for her, and sometimes I think she doesn't feel it the way we would."

Though Countess Mary told Natasha that those Gospel words should be understood differently, looking at Sonya she had to agree with Natasha's explanation. It really did seem that Sonya didn't find her position difficult and had grown quite reconciled to her role as a sterile flower. She seemed to value not individual people so much as the family as a whole. Like a cat, she had attached herself not to the people but to the house. She looked after the old countess, petted and spoiled the children, and was always ready to perform the small services she was capable of. But all this was accepted with too little gratitude...
The country house at Bald Hills had been rebuilt, though not on the same scale as under the old prince.

The buildings, begun under tight finances, were more than simple. The enormous house on the old stone foundations was of wood, plastered only on the inside. It had bare pine floors and was furnished with very plain hard sofas, armchairs, tables, and chairs made by their own serf carpenters from their own birch trees. The house was spacious, with rooms for the house serfs and quarters for visitors. Whole families of Rostov and Bolkonsky relatives would sometimes come to Bald Hills with sixteen horses and dozens of servants and stay for months. And four times a year—on the name days and birthdays of the heads of the household—as many as a hundred guests would gather for a day or two. The rest of the year, life went on in its unbroken routine, with its customary round of occupations—teas, breakfasts, dinners, and suppers—all provided from the estate's own produce.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: It was the eve of St. Nicholas Day, December fifth, 1820. That year Natasha and her husband and children had been staying at her brother's since early autumn. Pierre had gone to Petersburg on business "for three weeks," as he said, but had now been away for seven. He was expected back any minute.
Besides the Bezukhov family, Nicholas's old friend the retired General Vasili Dmitrich Denisov was also staying with the Rostovs on this fifth of December.

On the sixth—his name day, when the house would be full of visitors—Nicholas knew he would have to swap his Tatar tunic for a dress coat, put on narrow boots with pointed toes, and drive to the new church he had built, then receive congratulations and offer refreshments and talk about the local elections and the year's harvest. But the day before, he considered himself entitled to spend as he usually did. Before dinnertime Nicholas went over the bailiff's accounts from the Ryazan estate belonging to his wife's nephew, wrote two business letters, and strolled through the granaries, the cattle yard, and the stables. After taking measures against the general drunkenness expected the next day because of the holiday, he came in to dinner without having had a moment alone with his wife all day. He sat down at the long table laid for twenty people, around which the whole household was assembled. This included his mother, Sonya (who lived with them), his wife, their three children, their governess, their tutor, his wife's nephew with his tutor, and several others who always dined at the house.

Countess Mary sat at the other end of the table. When her husband sat down, she could tell from the quick way he grabbed his napkin and pushed aside the glass and wineglass in front of him that he was in a bad mood—as sometimes happened, especially before soup and when he came straight from work to the table. Countess Mary knew this mood well and, when she was in a good mood herself, would wait quietly until he had his first spoonful of soup, and only then begin talking—making him admit he had been in a bad mood for no reason. But today she entirely forgot this observation of hers; she felt hurt that he was cross with her for no reason, and she felt miserable. She asked him where he had been. He told her. She then asked whether all was going well on the estate. His frown deepened at her unnatural tone, and he answered briefly.

"So I'm not mistaken," thought Countess Mary. "But why is he cross with me?" She concluded from his tone that he was annoyed with her and wanted to end the conversation. She knew her remarks sounded forced, but couldn't help asking a few more questions.

Thanks to Denisov the conversation at dinner soon became general and lively, and she stopped talking to her husband. When they rose from the table and went as usual to thank the old countess, Countess Mary held out her hand and kissed her husband, asking him why he was angry with her.
"You always have such odd ideas! I didn't even think of being angry," he replied.
But the word "always" seemed to her to mean: "Yes, I am angry, but I won't tell you why."

Nicholas and his wife lived together so happily that even Sonya and the old countess—who felt jealous and would have liked them to disagree—could find nothing to criticize. But they too had their moments of tension. Occasionally, especially right after their happiest periods, a feeling of estrangement and hostility would come over them. This feeling occurred most often when Countess Mary was pregnant. She was pregnant now.

"Well, ladies and gentlemen," Nicholas said loudly and with forced cheerfulness—or so it seemed to Countess Mary, who felt he did it on purpose to annoy her—"I've been on my feet since six this morning. Tomorrow I'll have to suffer through the celebrations, so today I'm going to rest." And without a word to his wife, he went into the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.
And without a word to his wife he went to the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.

"That's always the way," thought Countess Mary. "He talks to everyone except me. I can see... I can see that I repel him, especially in this condition." She looked down at her pregnant figure and into the mirror at her pale, sallow, emaciated face with its larger-looking eyes.
And everything irritated her—Denisov's loud voice and laughter, Natasha's chatter, and especially the quick glance Sonya gave her.
Sonya was always the first excuse Countess Mary found for feeling irritated.
Having sat with the visitors for a while without following a word of what they said, she quietly left the room and went to the nursery.

The children were playing "going to Moscow" in a carriage made of chairs and invited her to join them. She sat down and played with them for a little while, but the thought of her husband and his unreasonable ill temper kept nagging at her. She got up and walked on tiptoe, with difficulty, to the small sitting room.
"Maybe he's not asleep. I'll have it out with him," she told herself. Little Andrew, her eldest boy, was following her on tiptoe, imitating his mother. She didn't notice him.
"Mary, dear, I think he's asleep—he was so tired," said Sonya, meeting her in the large sitting room. (It seemed to Countess Mary that Sonya crossed her path everywhere.) "Andrew might wake him."

Countess Mary looked around, saw little Andrew following her, felt that Sonya was right, and for that very reason flushed and with obvious difficulty kept herself from saying something sharp. She said nothing, but—to avoid obeying Sonya—beckoned Andrew to follow her quietly, and went to the door. Sonya went out by the other door. From the room where Nicholas lay asleep, his wife could hear his even breathing, every note of which was familiar to her. As she listened, she could see his smooth, handsome forehead and mustache, and the whole face she had studied so often in the silence of the night when he slept. Nicholas suddenly stirred and cleared his throat. And at that moment, little Andrew shouted from outside the door: "Papa! Mama's standing here!" Countess Mary paled with fright and began signaling to the boy. He fell silent, and for a moment there was a terrible stillness that lasted about a minute. She knew how much Nicholas disliked being woken. Then behind the door she heard another throat-clearing and a movement, and his displeased voice said:
"I can't get a moment's peace... Mary, is that you? Why did you bring him here?"
"I only came to look and didn't notice... I'm sorry..."

Nicholas coughed and said no more. Countess Mary moved away from the door and took the boy back to the nursery. Five minutes later, little black-eyed three-year-old Natasha—her father's pet—having learned from her brother that Papa was asleep and Mama was in the sitting room, ran to her father unnoticed by her mother. The dark-eyed little girl boldly pushed open the creaking door, marched to the sofa with determined little steps, and—seeing that her father was asleep with his back to her—stood on tiptoe and kissed the hand he was resting his head on. Nicholas turned around with a tender smile on his face.
"Natasha, Natasha!" came Countess Mary's frightened whisper from the door. "Papa wants to sleep."
"No, Mama, he doesn't want to sleep," said little Natasha with conviction. "He's laughing."
Nicholas swung his legs down, sat up, and took his daughter in his arms.
"Come in, Mary," he said to his wife.
She came in and sat down beside her husband.
"I didn't notice him following me," she said timidly. "I just looked in."
Holding his little girl with one arm, Nicholas glanced at his wife, and seeing her guilty expression, put his other arm around her and kissed her hair.
"May I kiss Mama?" he asked Natasha.
Natasha smiled shyly.
"Again!" she commanded with a bossy gesture, pointing to the spot where Nicholas had placed the kiss.
"I don't know why you think I'm cross," said Nicholas, answering the question he knew was in his wife's mind.
"You have no idea how unhappy, how lonely I feel when you're like that. It always seems to me—"
"Mary, don't be silly. You should be ashamed of yourself!" he said cheerfully.
"It seems to me that you can't love me, that I'm so plain... always... and now... in this state—"

"Oh, how ridiculous you are! It's not beauty that makes us love—it's love that makes us see beauty. It's only the Malvinas of the world who are loved for their looks. Do I love my wife? I don't just love her—but... I don't know how to put it. Without you, or when something comes between us like today, I feel completely lost—I can't do anything. Do I love my finger? No, but just try cutting it off..."
"I'm not like that myself, but I understand. So you're not angry with me?"
"Terribly angry!" he said, smiling. And he stood up, smoothed his hair, and began pacing the room.
"Do you know, Mary, what I've been thinking?" he began, immediately thinking aloud in his wife's presence now that they had made up.
He didn't ask if she was ready to listen. He didn't care. A thought had occurred to him and so it belonged to her too. And he told her his plan to convince Pierre to stay with them until spring.
Countess Mary listened until he had finished, made a comment, and in turn began thinking aloud. Her thoughts were about the children.

"You can already see the woman in her," she said in French, pointing to little Natasha. "You men accuse us women of being illogical. Here's our logic. I say: 'Papa wants to sleep!' but she says, 'No, he's laughing.' And she was right," said Countess Mary with a happy smile.

"Yes, yes." And Nicholas, taking his little daughter in his strong hand, lifted her high, set her on his shoulder, held her by the legs, and paced the room. Father and daughter wore identical expressions of carefree happiness.
"But you know, you may be unfair. You're too fond of this one," his wife whispered in French.
"Yes, but what can I do?... I try not to show it..."
At that moment they heard the sound of the door-pull and footsteps in the hall and front room, as if someone had arrived.
"Someone's here."
"I'm sure it's Pierre. I'll go and see," said Countess Mary, and she left the room.

In her absence, Nicholas allowed himself to give his little daughter a gallop around the room. Out of breath, he quickly lifted the laughing child from his shoulder and pressed her to his heart. His capering reminded him of dancing, and looking at the child's round, happy little face, he thought of what she would be like when he was an old man, taking her to balls, and he imagined her dancing the mazurka with some lanky young man, just as his late father-in-law had once danced Daniel Cooper with his daughter.

"It's him, it's him, Nicholas!" said Countess Mary, coming back a few minutes later. "Now our Natasha has come to life. You should have seen her face light up, and how she scolded him for staying away so long. Well, come along now, quick, quick! Separate yourselves at last!" she said, smiling as she looked at the little girl pressed against her father.
Nicholas went out, holding the child by the hand.
Countess Mary stayed behind in the sitting room.

"I would never, never have believed anyone could be so happy," she whispered to herself. A smile lit up her face, but at the same time she sighed, and a quiet sadness showed in her deep eyes—as though she felt, through her happiness, that there is another kind of happiness, unattainable in this life, which she could not help thinking of at that moment.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Natasha had married in the early spring of 1813, and by 1820 she already had three daughters and a son she had longed for and was now nursing. She had grown heavier and broader, so that it was hard to recognize the slim, lively Natasha of earlier years in this robust, motherly woman. Her features had settled and wore an expression of calm softness and serenity. Her face no longer had that ever-burning fire of eagerness that had been her chief charm. Now you often saw only her face and body, and her soul was not visible at all. All that could be seen was a strong, beautiful, and fertile woman. Very rarely now did the old fire blaze up—only when her husband came home, or a sick child recovered, or when she and Countess Mary talked about Prince Andrew (she never spoke of him to her husband, assuming he was jealous of Prince Andrew's memory), and very rarely when something happened to draw her into singing, which she had entirely given up after her marriage. And at those rare moments when the old fire did kindle, she was even more attractive than before, because of her new stateliness.

Since their marriage, Natasha and her husband had lived in Moscow, in Petersburg, on their estate near Moscow, and at her mother's house—that is, at Nicholas's. The young Countess Bezukhova was not often seen in society, and those who did see her were not impressed. She was neither charming nor agreeable. Not that Natasha liked solitude—she didn't really know whether she liked it or not, and in fact rather thought she didn't—but bearing, nursing, and raising children, and sharing every moment of her husband's life, meant that she could only satisfy those needs by giving up society. Everyone who had known Natasha before her marriage was surprised at the change in her, as though it were something extraordinary. Only the old countess, who—with her mother's instinct—understood that all of Natasha's outbursts had been nothing more than the need for a family, for a husband (as Natasha herself had said, more in earnest than in jest, at Otradnoe)—only the old countess was not surprised. She would say that she had always known Natasha would make a model wife and mother.
"Only she lets her love for her husband and children overflow all bounds," the countess said, "until it actually becomes ridiculous."

Natasha did not follow the golden rule urged by clever people, especially the French, which says that a girl should not let herself go after marriage, should not neglect her accomplishments, should be even more careful of her appearance than when she was single, and should charm her husband just as she had charmed him before. Natasha, on the contrary, had immediately abandoned all her accomplishments, among which the greatest was her singing. She gave it up precisely because it was such a powerful charm. She no longer bothered with her manners or her graceful ways of speaking, or with showing herself to her husband in the most flattering positions, or with avoiding boring him. She did the exact opposite of all that. She felt that the charms instinct had taught her to use before would now seem ridiculous to her husband, to whom she had given herself completely from the very first moment—that is, with her entire soul, leaving no corner of it hidden from him. She felt that the bond between her and her husband rested not on those romantic feelings that had attracted him to her, but on something else—something indefinite but firm, like the bond between her own soul and her body.

To curl her hair, put on fashionable dresses, and sing romantic songs to captivate her husband would have struck her as absurd—like decorating herself to attract herself. To dress up for others might perhaps have been pleasant—she didn't know—but she had no time for it. The main reason she didn't attend to her singing, her appearance, or even to the way she spoke was that she genuinely had no time for any of that.

We know that people have the ability to become completely absorbed in a subject, however trivial, and that there is no subject so trivial that it won't grow to infinite proportions if you devote your full attention to it.

The subject that wholly absorbed Natasha was her family: her husband, whom she had to keep so that he belonged entirely to her and to the home, and the children she had to carry, give birth to, nurse, and raise.

And the deeper she penetrated—not just with her mind but with her whole being—into the subject that absorbed her, the larger it grew and the less adequate her powers seemed, so she focused all her energy on the one thing and still could not accomplish everything she considered necessary.

Conversations and debates about women's rights—the relations of husband and wife, their freedom and obligations—existed then just as they do now, though they weren't yet called "questions." But these topics were not merely uninteresting to Natasha; she positively did not understand them. These questions, then as now, existed only for people who saw nothing in marriage except the pleasure the couple got from each other—that is, only the beginning of marriage, not its full significance, which lies in the family.

These questions, then as now, existed only for those who see nothing in marriage but the pleasure married people get from one another—that is, only the beginning of marriage and not its whole meaning, which lies in the family.

Debates of this kind—which are like the question of how to get the most enjoyment from your dinner—did not then and do not now exist for those whose purpose at dinner is nourishment; and the purpose of marriage is the family.
If the purpose of dinner is to nourish the body, a person who eats two dinners at once may get more enjoyment but won't achieve his purpose, because his stomach can't digest two dinners.
If the purpose of marriage is the family, then a person who wants many wives or husbands may get a great deal of pleasure, but will never have a real family.

If the purpose of food is nourishment and the purpose of marriage is the family, then the whole question comes down to: don't eat more than you can digest, and don't have more wives or husbands than you need for a family—that is, one wife or one husband. Natasha needed a husband. A husband was given to her. And the husband gave her a family. She not only saw no need for another, better husband, but since all the powers of her soul were devoted to serving that husband and family, she couldn't even imagine—and saw no point in imagining—what it would be like if things were different.

Natasha didn't care for society in general but valued all the more the company of her relatives—Countess Mary, her brother, her mother, and Sonya. She prized the company of people she could visit in her dressing gown, striding disheveled from the nursery with a joyful face to show a diaper with a yellow stain instead of a green one, and to hear reassuring words that the baby was now much better.

Natasha had let herself go to such an extent that her clothes, her badly chosen words, and her jealousy—she was jealous of Sonya, of the governess, of every woman, pretty or plain—were habitual subjects of jokes among those around her. The general opinion was that Pierre was under his wife's thumb, and this was indeed the case. From the very first days of their marriage, Natasha had made her demands known. Pierre was quite astonished by his wife's view—so completely new to him—that every moment of his life belonged to her and the family. His wife's demands astonished him, but they also flattered him, and he submitted.

Pierre's submission meant that he dared not only not flirt with but not even speak with a smile to any other woman, dared not dine at the club just for amusement, dared not spend money on a whim, and dared not be away for any length of time except on business—in which his wife included his intellectual pursuits, which she understood nothing about but attributed great importance to. In return, Pierre had the full right to run the whole household according to his wishes. In their own home Natasha made herself Pierre's slave, and the whole household had to go on tiptoe when Pierre was reading or writing in his study. Pierre had only to show a preference and the thing he wished was done. He had only to express a wish and Natasha jumped up to carry it out.

The entire household was governed according to Pierre's supposed wishes—that is, by his preferences, which Natasha tried to guess. Their way of life, their place of residence, their acquaintances and social connections, Natasha's occupations, the children's upbringing—all followed not only Pierre's expressed wishes but Natasha's attempts to deduce what those wishes were from ideas he had expressed in conversation. And she quite accurately identified his real wishes, and once she had found them she held to them firmly. When Pierre himself wanted to change his mind, she fought him with his own weapons.

For instance, during a difficult time that Pierre would always remember—after the birth of their first child, who was sickly, and they had to change wet nurses three times, and Natasha fell ill from despair—Pierre one day told her about Rousseau's view (which he entirely agreed with) that having a wet nurse was unnatural and harmful. With their next baby, despite opposition from her mother, the doctors, and her husband himself, who was alarmed by the idea of his wife nursing and regarded it as something outrageous, she insisted on nursing the baby herself, and from then on nursed all her children.

It happened quite often that in a moment of irritation, husband and wife would argue; but long afterward Pierre would discover—to his surprise and delight—that in his wife's ideas and actions he found the very thought she had argued against, stripped of everything extraneous that his own masculine expression of it had introduced. And he found it there in its purest form.

After seven years of marriage, Pierre had the joyful and firm conviction that he was not a bad man, and he felt this because he saw himself reflected in his wife. He felt the good and bad within himself all mixed together and overlapping. But only what was truly good was reflected in his wife: everything that wasn't perfectly good was rejected. And this reflection came about not through logical thought but through a different, mysterious, and direct process.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: Two months earlier, while Pierre was already staying with the Rostovs, he had received a letter from Prince Theodore asking him to come to Petersburg to confer on important matters being discussed by a society of which Pierre was one of the principal leaders.

On reading this letter—she always read her husband's letters—Natasha herself suggested that he go to Petersburg, though she would feel his absence deeply. She attributed immense importance to everything her husband did in the intellectual and abstract sphere, and was constantly afraid of being a hindrance to him in such matters. Pierre's timid, questioning look after reading the letter she met with a request that he go but set a definite date for his return. He was given four weeks' leave.
Since that leave had expired, more than two weeks ago now, Natasha had been in a constant state of alarm, depression, and irritability.

Denisov—now a retired general and very dissatisfied with the current state of affairs—had arrived during that fortnight. He looked at Natasha with sorrow and surprise, as at a bad likeness of someone once dear. A dull, dejected expression, random replies, and chatter about the nursery was all he saw and heard from his former enchantress.
Natasha was sad and irritable the whole time, especially when her mother, her brother, Sonya, or Countess Mary tried to console her by making excuses for Pierre and suggesting reasons for his delay.
"It's all nonsense, all rubbish—those discussions that lead nowhere and those stupid societies!" Natasha would say about the very causes she firmly believed to be of immense importance.

And she would go to the nursery to nurse Petya, her only boy. No one else could say anything as comforting or as sensible as what this little three-month-old creature communicated when he lay at her breast and she felt the movement of his lips and the snuffling of his tiny nose. That creature said: "You're angry, you're jealous, you want to get back at him, you're afraid—but I am he. I am he..." And there was no answer to that. It was more than true.

During that anxious fortnight, Natasha turned to the baby for comfort so often, and fussed over him so much, that she overfed him and he fell ill. She was terrified by his illness, and yet that was exactly what she needed. Looking after him let her bear her worry about her husband more easily.

She was nursing the baby when the sound of Pierre's sleigh was heard at the front door, and the old nurse—knowing how to please her mistress—came into the room silently but quickly, with a beaming face.
"Has he come?" Natasha asked in a rapid whisper, afraid to move and wake the dozing baby.
"He's here, ma'am," the nurse whispered.

Blood rushed to Natasha's face and her feet instinctively moved, but she couldn't jump up and run. The baby opened his eyes again and looked at her. "You're here?" he seemed to say, and lazily smacked his lips again.

Carefully pulling her breast free, Natasha rocked him a little, handed him to the nurse, and hurried with quick steps toward the door. But at the door she stopped, as if her conscience reproached her for leaving the child too soon in her joy. She glanced back. The nurse, with her elbows raised, was lifting the baby over the railing of his crib.
"Go, ma'am! Don't worry, go!" she whispered, smiling, with the kind of familiarity that develops between a nurse and her mistress.
Natasha ran with light footsteps to the front hall.
Denisov, who had come out of the study into the ballroom with his pipe, now for the first time recognized the old Natasha. A flood of brilliant, joyful light poured from her transformed face.
"He's come!" she called out as she ran past, and Denisov felt that he too was delighted Pierre had returned—Pierre, whom he didn't much care for.

Reaching the vestibule, Natasha saw a tall figure in a fur coat unwinding his scarf. "It's him! It's really him! He's here!" she said to herself, and rushing at him she embraced him, pressed his head to her chest, then pushed him back to look at his snow-dusted, rosy, happy face. "Yes, it's him. Happy and content—"
And all at once she remembered the anguish and suspense of the last two weeks. The joy that had lit up her face vanished; she frowned and poured a torrent of reproaches and angry words over Pierre.

"Yes, it's all very well for you. You're happy, you've been enjoying yourself... But what about me? You might at least have thought of the children. I'm nursing and my milk went bad... Petya nearly died. But you were having a good time. Yes, a good time!"

Pierre knew he wasn't to blame, since he couldn't have come sooner; he knew this outburst was unreasonable and would blow over in a minute or two; above all, he knew that he himself was bright and happy. He wanted to smile but didn't dare even think of doing so. He put on a pitiful, frightened expression and hunched over.
"I couldn't, on my honor. But how is Petya?"
"He's fine now. Come on! I can't believe you're not ashamed! If only you could see what I was like without you, how I suffered!"
"Are you well?"
"Come, come!" she said, not letting go of his arm. And they went to their rooms.

When Nicholas and his wife came to find Pierre, he was in the nursery holding his baby son—who was awake again—on his huge right palm, bouncing him gently. A blissfully bright smile was fixed on the baby's broad face with its toothless open mouth. The storm had long since passed, and Natasha's face was radiant with a sunny happiness as she watched her husband and child.
"And have you talked everything over with Prince Theodore?" she asked.
"Perfectly."
"You see—he's holding his head up." (She meant the baby's head.) "But how he frightened me... Have you seen the princess? Is it true she's in love with that—"
"Yes, can you imagine..."

At that moment Nicholas and Countess Mary came in. Pierre, with the baby on his arm, stooped to kiss them and answered their questions. But despite having much to discuss, the baby in his little cap, with his wobbly head, clearly took up all the attention Pierre could spare.

"How sweet!" said Countess Mary, looking at the baby and playing with him. "Now, Nicholas," she added, turning to her husband, "I can never understand how you don't see the charm of these darling little creatures."
"I don't and I can't," replied Nicholas, looking coldly at the baby. "A lump of flesh. Come along, Pierre!"
"And yet he's such a loving father," said Countess Mary, defending her husband. "But only after they're a year old or so..."
"Pierre nurses them beautifully," said Natasha. "He says his hand was made to be a baby's seat. Just look!"
"Only not for this..." Pierre suddenly exclaimed with a laugh, and shifting the baby, he handed him to the nurse.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: As in every large household, there were at Bald Hills several perfectly distinct worlds that merged into one harmonious whole, though each kept its own character and made allowances for the others. Every event—joyful or sad—that took place in the house was equally important in all these worlds, but each world had its own particular reasons for rejoicing or grieving about any given event.
Pierre's return, for instance, was a joyful and important event, and everyone felt it.

The servants—the most reliable judges of their masters, because they judge not by conversation or expressions of feeling but by actions and way of life—were glad Pierre was back because they knew that when he was there, Count Nicholas would stop going around the estate every day and would be more cheerful and good-humored, and also because everyone would get generous presents for the holidays.

The children and their governesses were glad of Pierre's return because no one else drew them into the social life of the household the way he did. He alone could play on the clavichord that one piece—his ecossaise—to which, as he said, every dance ever invented could be danced, and he had surely brought presents for everyone.

Young Nicholas—now a slim boy of fifteen, delicate and intelligent, with curly light-brown hair and beautiful eyes—was delighted because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous and passionate devotion. No one had deliberately tried to inspire this devotion in him; he had come to it on his own. In his imagination, Pierre was a hero. From half-remembered stories about Pierre and Natasha, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of the boy's dead father, from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy—who was only just beginning to guess what love is—formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha and had, when dying, bequeathed her to his friend. And that father—whom the boy did not remember—seemed to him a divinity who could not be imagined in human form, and of whom he never thought without a swelling heart and tears of sorrow and enthusiasm. So the boy was happy that Pierre had come.

From scattered remarks about Natasha and his father, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of the dead man, from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy—just beginning to understand love—concluded that his father had loved Natasha and had, in dying, entrusted her to his friend. And that father whom the boy didn't remember became in his mind a divinity beyond human form, and he never thought of him without a swelling heart and tears of sorrow and exaltation. And so the boy was glad Pierre had come.
The guests welcomed Pierre because he always helped to enliven and unite any company he was in.
The adult members of the family, not to mention his wife, were pleased to have a friend back whose presence made life flow more smoothly and peacefully.
The old ladies were pleased with the presents he brought, and especially that Natasha would now be herself again.
Pierre sensed these different attitudes from the various worlds in the household and made haste to satisfy everyone's expectations.

Though he was the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre had managed—with the help of a list his wife had drawn up—to buy everything, not forgetting his mother-in-law's and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material as a gift for Belova, nor toys for his nephews. In the early days of his marriage, this demand that he remember everything had struck him as strange, and he'd been impressed by the serious way Natasha insisted that he not forget a single item she'd entrusted to him, and by how offended she was when he returned from his first trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew accustomed to it. Knowing that Natasha never asked him to buy anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he offered, he now took an unexpected, childlike pleasure in buying presents for the whole household—never forgetting anything. If he deserved a scolding from Natasha, it was only for buying too many things and things that were too expensive.

Since Pierre had begun living as a family man—a life that entailed heavy expenses—he had noticed to his surprise that he spent only half as much as before, and that his finances, which had lately been in disorder (mainly because of his first wife's debts), were beginning to improve.

Living was cheaper because it was regulated: the most expensive luxury of all—the kind of life that can change at any moment—was no longer his, nor did he want it. He felt that his way of life was now settled once and for all until death, and that to change it was not in his power; and so this way of life proved cheap.
With a cheerful, smiling face Pierre was sorting through his purchases.
"What do you think of this?" he said, unrolling a piece of fabric like a shopkeeper.
Natasha, who was sitting across from him with her eldest daughter on her lap, quickly turned her sparkling eyes from her husband to the things he was showing her.
"That's for Belova? Wonderful!" She felt the material. "I'll bet it was a ruble a yard?"
Pierre told her the price.

"Too much!" Natasha remarked. "The children and Mama will be so pleased though! Only you shouldn't have bought this for me," she added, unable to suppress a smile as she admired a gold comb set with pearls, the kind that was just coming into fashion.
"Adele kept tempting me—she kept telling me to buy it," Pierre said.
"When would I wear it?" And Natasha stuck it in her hair. "When I take little Masha into society? Maybe these will be back in style by then. Well—let's go now."
And gathering up the presents, they went first to the nursery and then to the old countess's rooms.
The countess was sitting with her companion Belova, playing patience as usual, when Pierre and Natasha came into the drawing room with packages in their arms.
The countess was now over sixty, completely gray, and wore a cap with a frill that framed her face. Her face had shriveled, her upper lip had sunk in, and her eyes were dim.

After the deaths of her son and husband in such quick succession, she felt like a being accidentally left behind in this world, forgotten and without any purpose or reason for existing. She ate, drank, slept or lay awake, but she did not live. Life gave her no impressions. She wanted nothing from life except peace, and that peace she could only find in death. But until death came, she had to go on living—that is, using her vital forces. What could be clearly observed in very young children—the need to exercise all their faculties—was visible in her too in the highest degree. She needed to eat, sleep, think, talk, cry, work, get angry, and so on, simply because she had a stomach, a brain, muscles, nerves, and a liver. She did all these things not because anything prompted her from outside, as people in the prime of life do—when the purpose behind the exercise of their faculties is hidden by the aim to which those faculties are directed. She talked only because she physically needed to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried like a child because she needed to clear her nose, and so on.
So in the morning—especially if she'd eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and she would pick the handiest target: Belova's deafness.
She would say something to her in a low voice from the other end of the room.
"It seems a little warmer today, my dear," she would murmur.
And when Belova replied: "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another excuse would be her snuff, which was too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew by infallible signs when Belova would again be deaf, the snuff damp, and the countess's face yellow. Just as she needed to exercise her tongue, she sometimes needed to exercise her remaining capacity for thought—and the excuse for that was patience. When she needed to cry, the late count was the excuse. When she needed to feel anxious, Natasha's health was the excuse. When she needed to be sharp and angry, the excuse was Countess Mary. When she needed to exercise her voice—which usually happened around seven, after her after-dinner rest in a darkened room—the excuse was telling the same stories to the same audience over and over.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it, and they all made every possible effort to satisfy her needs. Only by a rare glance exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary did they reveal to each other their shared understanding of her state.

But those glances expressed something more: they said that she had played her part in life, that what they now saw was not her whole self, that we must all become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to restrain themselves for the sake of this once-dear creature who had been as full of life as they were now.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid members of that household, and the little children failed to understand this and avoided her.
